newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US rates to drift higher in Q1, then wane.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US rates to drift higher in Q1, then wane.

text.p: U.S. medium- and long-term government bond yields will rise by the end of this quarter, but will begin to fade lower in quarters ahead, according to experts polled in a Reuters quarterly economic survey.

On average, experts surveyed last week forecast the 30-year Treasury bond's yield to rise to 6.95 percent by the end of fourth-quarter 1996, hold steady for a quarter, then slip continuously toward 6.51 percent by the end of third-quarter 1998.

Forecasts for the two-year note paint a similar picture, but with even more dramatic declines in yield. After hovering near 6.15 percent for the next five quarters, the two-year yield is expected to fall sharply to 5.64 percent by the end of third-quarter 1998.
Citing expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike by early 1997, a majority of the experts forecast Treasury yields to steepen in the near term.
Don Ratajczak, director of the economic forecasting center at Georgia State University, said an initial rise in bond yields will be a direct reaction to monetary restraint.

With the economy growing slightly above its theoretical capacity, Ratajczak said inflationary pressures may arise. The central bank will probably respond by lifting the federal funds rate at its November 13 policy meeting, which will result in a flatter yield curve and slower economic growth.

If the Fed is passive or reluctant to stem inflationary pressures, wider yield spreads will occur "because that reluctance is viewed as being conciliatory with inflation, which is bad for long-term bond holders," he said.

As long as interest-rate policy makers act ahead of the market, they will be viewed as inflation fighters, and the long-bond yield will move down -- even as the Fed's action puts upward pressure on the short end of the market, explained Ratajczak.
"You will see a flattening, not an inversion, but a flattening of the yield curve," echoed Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors Inc.
The flattening will end when central bankers feel they have done the job and start to consider easing rates, said Chan.
The poll shows the Fed will likely start mulling that potential easing in the second quarter of 1997, after the Commerce Department releases first-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) data.

On average, the pundits predicted real GDP to grow at an annualized rate of 2.6 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, up from a projected 2.1-percent rate last quarter. But the economists forecast GDP growth to slip to 2.2 percent in first-quarter 1997.
Because the economy may need some time to recover from any near-term slowdown, the yield curve will remain flat, Chan explained.
Turning specifically to the long bond, Chan said the benchmark government security only reacts to strong inflationary pressures. "The long end will go down, but it won't go down big time."
